Laboratory colonies of the parasitic wasp Venturia canescens were maintained at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C] to establish baseline life-history parameters. Eggs deposited into host larvae possess an exceedingly modest initial dry weight, calculated from micrographic measurements as 0.000000187 grams , a value derived from assuming a cylindrical egg shape with a length of 0.027 centimeters and a radius of 0.0024 centimeters, and using a conservative tissue density of 0.4 grams per cubic centimeter. This remarkably low mass reflects the yolk-limited reserves available to the embryo. Upon hatching, the first-instar larva exhibits a dry weight of 0.000069 grams , representing a substantial multiplicative increase in mass from the egg stage. These measurements were obtained from cohorts of individuals reared on the factitious host Ephestia kuehniella and provide a crucial baseline for subsequent comparisons of growth efficiency across the larval and pupal stages.

The timing of early developmental events in Venturia canescens was quantified under the standard thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Hatching, defined here as the transition from a free chorionate egg to the first exogenous feeding event, occurs after approximately 4.0 days [ab = approximately 4.0 days] after oviposition at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively rapid embryogenesis is characteristic of many endoparasitic ichneumonids, where developmental speed is under strong selection to outpace the host's immune defenses. Following emergence from the egg, the larva embarks on a feeding phase within the hemocoel of the lepidopteran host. The interval between hatching and the onset of pupation was recorded as 5.0 days after hatching  at this temperature at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This brief larval feeding period, during which the parasitoid consumes host tissues and accumulates the biomass necessary for metamorphosis, highlights the efficiency of resource extraction by this koinobiont species.

As the larval period concludes, the parasitoid undergoes a dramatic transformation. The dry weight of the individual at the moment of pupation was measured as 0.00477 grams . This represents the peak biomass achieved during the immature feeding phase, after which the animal ceases feeding and enters the non-feeding pupal stage, a quiescent period in which histolysis and imaginal disc expansion occur. The duration of this pupal resting stage, measured from the time of pupation to the emergence of the adult imago, was determined to be 10.0 days after pupation  under the standard conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This period encompasses the complete reorganisation of larval tissues into the adult form, culminating in the rupture of the puparium and the eclosion of the teneral adult.

Upon emergence from the puparium, the newly formed imago of Venturia canescens exhibits a dry weight of 0.00175 grams . This value is notably lower than the dry weight recorded at pupation, a discrepancy that reflects the substantial metabolic costs incurred during the metamorphic process, including the energy expended for histolysis, histogenesis, and the construction of adult flight musculature and exoskeleton. The teneral adult requires a brief period for cuticle hardening and wing expansion before it can commence host-searching and reproductive activities. When supplied with honey solution and maintained under constant conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the adult imago displays a maximum lifespan of 36.5 days [am = 36.5 days]. This adult longevity is sufficient to locate and parasitize multiple hosts during the reproductive phase, a key trait contributing to its efficacy as a biological control agent.

The life-history strategy of Venturia canescens is thus characterized by a rapid pre-adult development punctuated by significant shifts in both mass and form. From an initial egg dry weight of just 0.000000187 grams , the wasp accumulates biomass through active larval feeding, culminating in a pupal mass of 0.00477 grams , an increase of over four orders of magnitude. The metabolic cost of metamorphosis is evident in the reduction to an adult emergence weight of 0.00175 grams . The entire developmental sequence from egg to adult eclosion, comprising an egg incubation period of approximately 4.0 days [ab = approximately 4.0 days], a larval feeding phase of 5.0 days after hatching , and a pupal metamorphosis period of 10.0 days after pupation  at the controlled temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is completed in just 19 days. The resulting imago then has a reproductive window of 36.5 days [am = 36.5 days] to exploit available hosts at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].
